responses: After careful consideration of the group’s discussions, my final position is that we should allocate 35% to Workforce Training, 25% to Automation, 20% to Data Infrastructure, 10% to Employee Support, and 10% to the Innovation Lab. I believe this balance prioritizes our people first—ensuring they are equipped and supported through the transition—while still making meaningful investments in automation and the foundational data systems needed to sustain long-term efficiency and growth. The Innovation Lab and Employee Support, while valuable, should receive smaller shares to avoid spreading our $5 million budget too thin across too many fronts.

I would recommend a balanced allocation that prioritizes Workforce Training (30%) and Employee Support (20%) alongside Automation (25%) and Data Infrastructure (20%), with a smaller Innovation Lab (5%). The human side of this transition is critical—without reskilling and support, automation risks creating resistance, turnover, and morale problems that undermine efficiency gains. Investing in people first ensures we have the talent to operate new systems, while still dedicating substantial funds to automation and infrastructure to stay competitive. The Innovation Lab can be kept lean initially, focusing on low-cost experiments that inform future investments.

I’d tell them that after a lot of back-and-forth, I came to see that the smartest move for Riverton isn’t to go all-in on automation or just throw money at training—it’s about balance. I ended up pushing for a roughly 30% split between workforce training and employee support, because if we don’t help people adapt and feel secure, the new tech will just create resentment and turnover. Then I’d put about 25% into data infrastructure to make sure our systems can actually handle AI, 20% into automation for quick efficiency wins, and leave 25% for an innovation lab to keep us competitive long-term. It’s not perfect, but it’s a plan that tries to respect both the human side and the business side of this transition.

After careful consideration of the committee’s discussions, my final position is that we should allocate the $5 million budget with a strong emphasis on **Workforce Training (35%)** and **Employee Support (25%)**, followed by **Data Infrastructure (20%)**, **Automation (15%)**, and a smaller **Innovation Lab (5%)**. I believe that the human element is the most critical factor in a successful AI transition—without properly reskilling our workforce and providing robust support systems, we risk resistance, burnout, and talent loss. While automation and infrastructure are important, they will only deliver long-term value if our employees are equipped and motivated to work alongside new technologies. This balanced approach ensures we build both technical capacity and a resilient, engaged workforce.

I'd recommend a balanced but forward-leaning allocation: 30% to Automation, 25% to Workforce Training, 20% to Data Infrastructure, 15% to Innovation Lab, and 10% to Employee Support. Automation gives us immediate competitive gains and efficiency, which the board will expect to see from a $5 million investment. But without training and support, we risk alienating our workforce and creating a skills gap that undermines long-term success. Data infrastructure is the backbone that makes everything else work—if our systems can't handle AI, the other investments stall. The Innovation Lab keeps us future-focused, and Employee Support ensures we treat people fairly through the transition. This split prioritizes tangible results while protecting our human capital.

I’d tell them that after all the discussion, I came down firmly in favor of putting the largest share—about 35%—into workforce training, because no matter how good the AI tools are, they’re useless if people don’t know how to use them or feel threatened by them. I’d also allocate 25% to data infrastructure, since you can’t run AI without solid data systems and security. Then I’d split the rest: 20% to automation for quick efficiency wins, 15% to an innovation lab to explore new products, and just 5% to employee support, because I believe the best support is giving people the skills and tools to thrive in the new environment rather than just cushioning the transition.

This approach recognizes that our greatest asset is our workforce—without their buy-in and skills, the technology will fail—and that a gradual, human-centered transition will yield more sustainable long-term results than rushing into automation at the expense of employee morale and adaptability.
